name: Bordeaux
title: Ultrasonic Thickness Gauging Bordeaux | Gironde Ship UTM
description: Ship thickness measurement on the Gironde at Bordeaux, Bassens, Ambès, Pauillac and Le Verdon: tankers, bulkers, ro-ro and river-sea ships gauged by UTM.
h1: Hull and Tank Gauging on the Gironde, from Le Verdon to Bordeaux
intro: Bordeaux is a river port spread along the Gironde estuary and the Garonne, from the sea terminals at Le Verdon and Pauillac to Ambès, Bassens and the city quays. Tankers, bulkers, ro-ro ships and grain carriers all load or discharge along this chain. Superintendents ask for ultrasonic gauging when a ship is due a survey, needs steel readings before a docking, or has a charterer's request. The team is flown in from India to join the ship at the berth or anchorage.

highlights.p: Le Verdon, Pauillac, Ambès and Bassens each take different ship types. One mobilisation can cover several berths when a ship moves up river, which helps a superintendent whose vessel loads at more than one terminal.

highlights.h: Oil and chemical tankers at Ambès
highlights.p: Ambès handles petroleum and chemical products, and tankers arrive for loading or discharge with ballast tanks available between cargoes. That makes it a practical place for ballast tank and deck gauging ahead of vetting.
Ships moving up the Gironde work with tide and pilots, so berth times shift. Gauging plans for this port allow for the tide table and agent confirmation, rather than a fixed hour.

p: The Grand Port Maritime de Bordeaux does not sit on a single harbour. It is a string of terminals along the Gironde estuary and the Garonne river, running inland from the sea. Le Verdon-sur-Mer, at the mouth of the estuary, has the deep-water container, ro-ro and bulk berths and the first anchorage. Pauillac lies some way upstream and handles oil products and project cargo, with ro-ro ships carrying large aircraft components. Ambès, at the junction of the Garonne and the Dordogne, is the main oil and chemical hub, and Bassens, nearer the city, deals in grain, wood, fertiliser and general cargo.

Ship types follow the terminals. Product tankers, chemical tankers and small gas carriers use Ambès and Pauillac. Bulk carriers call for grain at Bassens and for fertiliser, coal and other bulk cargo at several quays. Ro-ro and ro-pax ships work at Le Verdon and Pauillac, and containers move through Le Verdon and Bassens. Wine, a historic trade for Bordeaux, travels today mostly in containers and in tankers carrying bulk wine, and a number of river cruise ships and small sea cruise ships call at the city quays during the season.

The estuary is wide, shallow in places and tidal, so draught limits and pilotage shape every movement. Ships anchor off Le Verdon to wait for the tide or for a berth, and transits upriver are timed to the flood. For gauging this means the team may join a ship at the first berth or at the roads and stay on board for a leg of the passage, or board only after the ship has moored. Which approach is workable depends on the ship's schedule, the pilot boarding arrangements and the agent's advice, and it is agreed before travel is booked.

Most gauging is done alongside at the working terminals. At Ambès and Pauillac the terminals operate strict permit-to-work systems for tankers, so ballast tanks and void spaces are entered only with the ship's enclosed-space permit and the terminal's agreement. At Bassens and the grain quays, bulk carriers can be gauged between discharge and loading, when the holds are clean and the ship's staff can release the spaces. Le Verdon is the practical choice for ro-ro and container ships and for anything waiting at anchor.

Bordeaux has a ship-repair tradition on the upstream side of the port, with repair quays and a dry dock used for river-sea ships, workboats and smaller merchant ships. Its present capacity should be confirmed with the port authority and the yard before it is built into a plan. For larger ships that need a dry docking, the owner usually looks to a yard on the Atlantic coast of Spain or elsewhere in France, and the Gironde call becomes the pre-docking gauging stop.
list: Le Verdon deep-water quays, for ro-ro, container and bulk ship gauging with launch access to the roads.
Pauillac oil and ro-ro berths, for ballast tank, deck and ramp gauging within terminal permit rules.
Ambès petroleum and chemical terminals, for tanker ballast tank and cofferdam gauging.
Bassens grain, wood and general cargo quays, for hold, hopper tank and hatch coaming gauging.
City quays at Bordeaux, for river cruise ships, small coasters and workboats alongside.
Estuary anchorage off Le Verdon, for work on ships waiting for the tide or a berth, weather permitting.

context.h: Port state control and shipping rules on the Gironde
p: France applies port state control under the Paris MoU, carried out by the maritime administration's ship safety centres, and ships at any Gironde terminal can be selected for inspection. For older tankers and bulkers, an inspector who finds heavy corrosion or deck wastage can raise deficiencies that delay sailing, so owners with ageing ships often commission gauging before the call rather than after a detention.

Several rules shape gauging demand here. Tankers loading at Ambès and Pauillac fall under the enhanced survey programme and the oil company vetting process, and chemical tankers face their own survey extent. The EU Ship Recycling Regulation requires an inventory of hazardous materials on ships calling at EU ports, EU ETS applies to emissions on voyages into and out of the Gironde, and FuelEU Maritime sets greenhouse gas intensity limits for fuel used on those calls. These do not change how steel is measured, but they push owners to look at ship condition when a ship's future trading is under review.

jobs.h: Typical gauging jobs on the Gironde
jobs.p: Jobs follow the cargoes and the ship's survey cycle, with the berth schedule setting the window. Because several terminals sit on the same river, a team can sometimes follow a ship from one berth to the next. Typical ultrasonic thickness gauging here includes:
list: Ballast tank and cofferdam gauging on a product tanker at Ambès, ahead of a vetting inspection.
Hold frame, hopper tank and hatch coaming gauging on a grain carrier at Bassens between discharge and loading.
Ramp, vehicle deck and ballast tank steel on a ro-ro ship at Pauillac during a short call.
Deck, bulwark and hull plating readings on a river cruise ship alongside at the city quays during the winter lay-up.
Pre-docking steel estimate on a coaster or chemical tanker before the yard slot is booked.

logistics: Bordeaux-Mérignac airport is the usual arrival point and sits within road reach of the upstream terminals and the estuary. Reaching Le Verdon or Pauillac takes a longer road transfer, which the agent helps plan. France is in the Schengen area, so each technician travels on a Schengen visa from India, and the lead time is driven by the visa rather than the road. Gate passes for each terminal are arranged by the ship's agent, and the port's access rules change from terminal to terminal.
vessels: River cruise and small sea cruise ships

faqs.q: Can one team gauge a ship at more than one Gironde terminal?
faqs.a: Yes, when the ship's schedule allows. If a vessel discharges at one berth and loads at another further up the river, the team can stay on board or join at the next berth. We agree the sequence with the agent and the superintendent, because tide and pilot arrangements decide when the ship moves.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock in Bordeaux for steel renewal?
faqs.a: The port has repair quays and a dock suited to smaller ships and workboats, though capacity changes and should be confirmed with the authority and the yard. Larger merchant ships normally dock elsewhere on the Atlantic coast, and the Gironde call is where pre-docking gauging gives the yard a steel estimate.

faqs.q: Can tankers be gauged at Ambès while cargo is being worked?
faqs.a: Only in spaces the terminal allows. Ballast tanks, voids and deck structure can sometimes be gauged at the berth with the terminal's agreement and the ship's permit, but never in cargo tanks during cargo operations. Many owners choose a gap between cargoes or a call without cargo for the cleaner access.

faqs.q: What if the ship is waiting at anchor off Le Verdon?
faqs.a: Gauging at anchor is possible in settled weather with a launch, and works best for ballast tanks and deck structure. Wind against tide in the estuary can make transfers unsafe, so we keep a fallback to the berth and rely on the agent's weather advice.

faqs.q: Can river cruise ships be gauged during winter lay-up?
faqs.a: Yes. Lay-up gives long access to ballast tanks, the hull and deck plating, and the work can be scheduled around the operator's maintenance programme. We agree the spaces with the technical manager, and readings are reported by location so wasted plating is easy to follow into the next season.
